contributions.headingText: Anal condyloma is a benign papillary squamous proliferation with a fibrovascular core, caused by HPV infection. Buschke–Lowenstein tumour (BLT) is a giant condyloma with features of deep growth and local destruction.
Condyloma occurs in the anal canal, anal transformation zone, anal skin, and perianal region. BLT is large and often involves tissue both inside and outside the anal canal.

Patients with condyloma may be asymptomatic or could present with anal discomfort or pruritus. The lesion may be solitary or multiple and may present as a cauliflower-like mass. Patients with BLT present with a large pushing mass, with fistulas, abscesses, bleeding, and displacement of adjacent tissue. A anoscopy with biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis. Radiological examination (CT or MRI) is used to exclude malignant transformation.

Condyloma is most common in young patients in the third decade of life {26602622}. The prevalence of anogenital condyloma is similar in men and women. Anal condyloma is more common in young men who have sex with men and HIV-positive individuals. In Australia, 4.5% of men who reported engaging in anoreceptive sex had anal condyloma {29420447}.

BLT (giant condyloma) may be seen in paediatric patients as young as 18 months of age {27384409}. Men are more commonly affected, with an M:F ratio of 2.7:1.

The etiology of condyloma and BLT is linked to HPV infection, usually (in > 90% of cases) the low oncogenic risk subtypes HPV6 and HPV11. Risk factors for acquiring the virus include immunodeficient state (HIV infection, after organ and bone marrow transplantation) and increased contacts (unprotected sex with multiple partners and anal intercourse) {25597932}. The virus can also be transmitted via surface-to-surface contact without sexual intercourse {24913124}.
HPV infection begins in the basal layer of stratified squamous epithelium, resulting in squamous proliferation of condyloma.

Condyloma appears as a warty tumour with an irregular surface. BLT is a giant condyloma, which may grow to 130 mm {28012208}. It is a destructive lesion, with a propensity for infections and fistulations.

Microscopically, condyloma is characterized by hyperplastic papillary squamous epithelium with parakeratosis and a fibrovascular core. The upper third of the squamous epithelium typically shows koilocytes. Coexisting squamous dysplasia or squamous cell carcinoma should be excluded. Condyloma without dysplasia is usually negative for p16 on immunohistochemistry {26994411}. Strong, block-like p16 staining is often noted in dysplasia and carcinoma with high-risk HPV subtypes.

Large condyloma must be differentiated from verrucous carcinoma and BLT {28012208}. Verrucous carcinoma invades the underlying stroma in the form of bulbous pegs with a pushing border. There is no koilocytosis or HPV in verrucous carcinoma {28012208}. BLT resembles condyloma histologically but has deep local extension and displacement of surrounding tissues {29644039}.

Squamous papilloma of anus is extremely rare {23526509}. It may represent a form of burned-out condyloma with no HPV detected.

Small condyloma must be distinguished from fibroepithelial polyp, which lacks papillary proliferation of squamous epithelium and does not show koilocytosis.
Essential: macroscopically, a warty lesion; histologically, epithelial hyperplasia with parakeratosis around fibrovascular cores (typically with koilocytes); no evidence of dysplasia.

Small condyloma can regress and be treated conservatively. Those located in the anal canal and distal end of the rectal ampulla require surgery {24913124}. Large condyloma and BLT do not regress spontaneously and are prone to recurrence and malignant transformation. Recurrence of anal condyloma ranges from 4.6% to > 70%, depending on the treatment modality {26937152}. The prevalence of high-grade dysplasia and carcinoma in patients with pre-existing anal condyloma is higher in HIV-positive patients {29183133}.
